entries.clue: Loose rope – vessel misses the alarm? (10)

indicatorNotes.Loose: Something loose is not tied down, and letters that are not tied down will not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, the dash between them only punctuation

annotation.surface: A ship with a slack line aboard, sleeping through the warning it should have answered.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loose' reads as a description of the rope and is the instruction instead, which is why the fodder is so hard to see sitting right beside it.
annotation.definitionFit: To oversleep is to stay asleep past the hour you set, which is what missing the alarm amounts to.

entries.clue: Supermarkets not opening? Oh dear! (4)

indicatorNotes.not opening: A word that is not opening has nothing at its front, so the letter it began with is gone.

blocks.note: the Co-op is a chain of British grocery shops, and more than one of them is spelt this way
the letter the five-letter word starts on, and the one that is thrown away

annotation.surface: A morning when the local shops all turn out to be shut.
annotation.walkthrough: The shops are the Co-op, a member-owned chain on British high streets, and the plural is what makes the word long enough. Removing a head letter is all the clue asks of you.
annotation.definitionFit: Oops is the small noise you make on realising you have made a mistake, the same reflex as oh dear.

entries.clue: Earl to go for duelling sword (4)

blocks.note: the single letter that stands for an earl in the peerage
to go, in the nursery sense of needing the lavatory

annotation.surface: An earl setting off to fetch the weapon he means to fight with.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To go' is the polite phrase for a trip to the lavatory, and that noise is what the second chunk spells. The épée is the heaviest of the three fencing weapons and the only one where the whole body counts as target.
annotation.definitionFit: The épée is the stiff-bladed fencing sword taken straight from the old duelling weapon, so 'duelling sword' names it by its ancestor.

entries.clue: As Spooner tells it, public school’s meat is a bird of prey (11)

indicatorNotes.As Spooner tells it: The Reverend Spooner's trademark slip was to exchange the opening sounds of two words as he said them, so the pair named here trade their fronts.

blocks.note: Harrow is one of England's oldest fee-paying boarding schools, on a hill north-west of London; said at speed its 's slides forward onto the next word
the meat is pork, and with that stray s in front of it the sp- sound is what goes back to the school

annotation.surface: Spooner announcing what a famous boarding school is serving for lunch.
annotation.walkthrough: Say 'Harrow's pork' aloud and hear where the s lands: it leans forward onto the meat, giving Spooner an sp- and an h- to exchange. The possessive doing that work is the part solvers miss.
annotation.definitionFit: A sparrowhawk is the small, fast raptor that hunts finches and tits through gardens and woodland, so 'a bird of prey' places it by trade.

entries.clue: Seeing back half of salter, in lane, reversing – it’s going on forever (7)

indicatorNotes.Seeing back half of: When only the back half of a word is on show, the letters it ends on are the ones you get to use.
indicatorNotes.in: 'In' puts the piece just named inside the word that follows rather than beside it.
indicatorNotes.reversing: Something reversing runs the other way, so the word's letters are read from its far end back.

blocks.note: the four letters of the narrow road, taken from the back end forwards
the word has six letters, so its back half is three of them

annotation.surface: Catching sight of a salt lorry backing down a lane, apparently taking all night about it.
annotation.walkthrough: A salter is the gritting lorry that spreads salt on winter roads, and the whole picture is there to keep you looking at traffic. Two separate instructions sit either side of one comma.
annotation.definitionFit: What is eternal has no end in either direction, so 'going on forever' is the plainest way to say it.

entries.clue: Rod’s to knock up root vegetable (7)

indicatorNotes.up: In a down entry the letters run downwards, so a piece sent up is read back from its foot to its head.

blocks.note: to knock at a door is to rap on it, and climbing the column that word arrives this way round
a rod is a pin, the clue's 's adds the letter after it, and the four together are read from the bottom up

annotation.surface: Rod on his way to bang on somebody's door.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rod' looks like a man's name because of the apostrophe, and it is a thing you fasten with. The 's is not decoration either: it is a letter of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A parsnip is the pale sweet root pulled from the ground and roasted like a carrot, so 'root vegetable' names it by kind.

entries.clue: Hot beverage, somewhat archaic (4)

indicatorNotes.somewhat: Somewhat means only part of it, so only part of the word that follows is wanted — the run of letters sitting together inside.

blocks.note: the letters wanted run consecutively inside this word, in the order they are printed

annotation.surface: Someone dismissing a hot drink as a bit old-fashioned.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Archaic' looks like a verdict on the drink and is the hiding place. Chai is simply the word for tea across much of Asia, taken into English for the spiced milky version sold here.
annotation.definitionFit: Chai is tea simmered with milk and spices and drunk hot, so 'hot beverage' names it by its category.

entries.clue: Monarch, one surrounded by hams, cracked joke with dirty ending (3,7)

indicatorNotes.cracked: A cracked thing has broken apart, and letters broken apart do not go back together in the order they came.
indicatorNotes.surrounded by: What is surrounded by something has that something closing on it from both sides.
indicatorNotes.ending: A word's ending is the single letter it finishes on.

blocks.note: the four letters of the cured meat, broken up and reset in this order
the Roman numeral for one is a single letter
a joke is a jest
the letter the word dirty finishes on

annotation.surface: A king telling a slightly blue joke with a plate of ham in front of him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cracked joke' reads as one phrase and belongs to two different pieces of the parse: the cracking is done to the hams, and the joke stands on its own. Four chunks for ten letters is a lot of assembly for a two-word title.
annotation.definitionFit: His Majesty is the formal style by which a reigning king is addressed, so the words stand in for the man himself.

entries.clue: To odiously fudge announcement after the event (1,4,3,2)

indicatorNotes.fudge: To fudge something is to mess about with it until it comes out other than it was, and that is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, the whole of the clue's opening

annotation.surface: Making a thoroughly unpleasant mess of an announcement that comes too late anyway.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder sits right at the front, where solvers expect a definition, and the split infinitive makes it read as instructions rather than as letters. The four-part enumeration is the best clue that a whole phrase is coming.
annotation.definitionFit: 'I told you so' is the line delivered once the predicted disaster has actually happened, so it is an announcement that arrives too late to be any use.

entries.clue: In Paris, Peter embraces girlfriend in townhouse? (4-1-5)

indicatorNotes.embraces: To embrace is to take into your arms, closing round whatever is being held.

blocks.note: 'in Paris' asks for the French, and Peter is Pierre there
the person you are seeing is your date

annotation.surface: A Frenchman called Pierre with his arms round his girlfriend in a smart house in town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' does not put anything anywhere: it tells you to translate. A pied-à-terre is literally a foot on the ground, the small flat kept for the occasional night in the city.
annotation.definitionFit: A pied-à-terre is a second home kept in town for occasional use, and the question mark admits that 'townhouse' names it loosely rather than exactly.

entries.clue: City consultor regularly ignored (4)

indicatorNotes.regularly ignored: What is ignored regularly is skipped at a steady interval, so every other letter of the word that follows drops out.

blocks.note: count through the nine letters dropping the first, the third, the fifth and so on, and keep what is left

annotation.surface: An adviser whose opinion gets passed over as a matter of routine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Consultor' is a real word rather than a misprint — an adviser, most often one attached to a Roman congregation — and the clue wants it only for its spelling.
annotation.definitionFit: Oslo is the capital of Norway, at the head of its own fjord, so 'City' names it by kind.

entries.clue: Location for evening dress? (7,5)

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: somewhere black tie and long frocks are kept or put on
the reading the setter means: the evening of a dress, evening being the act of making something flat and smooth

annotation.surface: Wondering where formal clothes are supposed to be kept.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Evening' is a noun in the surface and a verb underneath: to even something is to take the creases out of it. The question mark is the only warning that the phrase has been re-read.
annotation.definitionFit: An ironing board is the padded table a dress is laid flat on to be pressed, and pressing it is evening it out.

entries.clue: Time for shopping – badly, if rack damaged (5,6)

indicatorNotes.damaged: Something damaged has been knocked out of shape, and letters knocked out of shape no longer sit where they did.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder, three short words run together

annotation.surface: A shopping trip going wrong and a display rack broken in the process.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Badly' is the word most solvers seize on as the instruction, and it is fodder; the real instruction waits at the far end of the clue. The day itself is the American discount sale that British shops have taken up.
annotation.definitionFit: Black Friday is the late-November sale day, now kept on this side of the Atlantic too, given over entirely to bargain hunting.

entries.clue: Occasion hoping for bright ideas after British wet weather (10)

indicatorNotes.after: 'After' fixes which of the two pieces trails the other: the weather is what comes along behind, and the country's letter leads.

blocks.note: the single letter used for British on passports and number plates alike
heavy wet weather is a storm of rain, and the compound for it runs to nine letters

annotation.surface: British weather doing what it does, and somebody hoping for inspiration in spite of it.
annotation.walkthrough: The seam between the two pieces falls inside a single syllable, which is exactly what hides it: one letter, then one whole word. 'Bright ideas' is definition work, not wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A brainstorm is the session where a group throws out ideas as fast as they come in the hope that one of them is any good.

entries.clue: Tipsiness: so tiny crackers sandwiching French cheese (10)

indicatorNotes.crackers: Crackers is British slang for out of one's mind, and letters treated madly will not stay in the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.sandwiching: To sandwich something is to lay it between two layers, so what is named next goes inside rather than alongside.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, reset into this order so that a gap opens in the middle
the soft white-rinded cheese named after the region east of Paris

annotation.surface: Very small biscuits with a slice of French cheese laid between them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crackers' is the biscuit in the surface and the shuffling instruction in the parse, which is the whole of the misdirection. The cheese slots into the middle of the shuffled letters rather than onto either end.
annotation.definitionFit: Insobriety is the state of not being sober — being the worse for drink — which is what tipsiness names more lightly.

entries.clue: Recovered from gangrene, wallaby’s fresh start (7)

indicatorNotes.Recovered from: To recover something is to get it back out of wherever it is lying, and the words that follow are where it lies.

blocks.note: the letters wanted run straight on through the comma and the space between the two words

annotation.surface: A wallaby that has pulled through a nasty infection and is beginning again.
annotation.walkthrough: The span crosses a comma and a word boundary, which is where hidden words are hardest to spot. 'Recovered from gangrene' is a complete idea in the surface and half an instruction underneath it.
annotation.definitionFit: A renewal is a starting over — of a lease, a licence, a friendship — so 'fresh start' is the same idea in plainer words.

entries.clue: Location with unpleasant smell: its effect is psychological (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer instead of replacing it: the setter names the thing by the one fact everybody knows about it rather than offering a noun that could stand in its place.

blocks.note: a location is a place
BO is the standing short form of body odour, and nobody says the phrase in full

annotation.surface: A spot that smells bad, with the suggestion that the smell is all in your head.
annotation.walkthrough: The colon does the job a link word usually does: everything before it is wordplay, everything after it describes the answer. Two ordinary chunks join without any instruction at all.
annotation.definitionFit: A placebo is a dummy pill with no active ingredient in it, so any improvement the patient feels comes from believing in the treatment.

entries.clue: ‘I cry a river’: first of stanza’s lines showing who’s under pressure (7)

indicatorNotes.first of: The first of a word is the single letter it opens on, and nothing else of it is wanted.

blocks.note: the pronoun is taken at face value, one letter as printed
to cry is to sob
the article stands exactly as it is written
R is how a river is shortened on any map
the opening letter of the word for a poem's block of verse

annotation.surface: Someone quoting the song about crying a river, then counting off the lines of a poem.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Under pressure' is the giveaway once you stop reading it as stress: on a weather chart the phrase is literal. The quotation marks are surface decoration and carry no instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Isobars are the lines joining points of equal air pressure on a weather map, and whatever sits inside a deep low really is under it.

entries.clue: Tool for bridge? (7)

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: an implement wanted for building a river crossing, or for a game of cards
the reading the setter means: to bridge a gap is to span it, so what is wanted is a thing whose name says it spans

annotation.surface: Hunting for the right implement to get a bridge built.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is a joke on its own name: the -er ending turns a verb into the thing that performs it, and a spanner grips nuts rather than gaps. The question mark quietly admits no letters are being moved anywhere.
annotation.definitionFit: A spanner is the tool that turns a nut, and read as 'one that spans' it is also a description of what any bridge does.

entries.clue: Caribbean island offering halos, certificates of miracles, did you say? (2,5)

indicatorNotes.did you say?: 'Did you say?' asks you to trust your ears rather than the page, so what matters is the noise the words make, not their spelling.

blocks.note: a kit assembled for a saint would hold a halo and the paperwork proving the miracles, and said aloud that pair of words is the place wanted

annotation.surface: A shop somewhere warm selling haloes and miracle paperwork over the counter.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is a starter pack: everything a candidate for canonisation needs, sold as a set. Written down, the saint shrinks to its usual abbreviation and the kits pick up a second T.
annotation.definitionFit: St Kitts is the larger of the two islands of St Kitts and Nevis, in the eastern Caribbean, so the definition places it by its sea.

entries.clue: Primarily solid – perhaps heavenly, endlessly rotating in circles? (7)

annotation.definition: Primarily solid – perhaps heavenly, endlessly rotating in circles?

indicatorNotes.Primarily: What comes primarily comes first, so every word after it gives up the letter it opens on and nothing more.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the list's first word
even the hedging word hands over its first letter
the opening letter of the word heavenly, taken like the rest
the opening letter, despite the word looking like a deletion order
the opening letter of the word rotating, not an instruction to turn anything
the little preposition counts as a word and gives its front letter
the last of the list, handing over the letter it begins with

annotation.surface: A solid body somewhere out in the heavens, turning and turning and never stopping.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word after the first does two jobs at once: it describes the shape and hands over its opening letter, so nothing is left to serve as a separate definition. 'Endlessly' looks like a deletion order and is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes a planet or a star — solid, celestial, spinning without end — and those are the bodies the word describes.

entries.clue: Emulate xylophonist: ring any bells (6,1,5)

blocks.note: do what a xylophone player does: hit the bars so that several notes sound together
seem familiar, the way a half-remembered name does when somebody says it

annotation.surface: Asking whether playing the xylophone reminds you of anything at all.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are about sound, which is what makes the seam so hard to find: one is literal music, the other the idiom for a faint memory. No instruction word appears anywhere in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: To strike a chord is literally to sound several notes at once, which is the xylophonist's whole job, and figuratively to touch on something a listener already knows.

entries.clue: Apple computers lifted in con (4)

indicatorNotes.lifted: In a down entry the letters run downwards, so a piece lifted is read back up from its foot to its head.

blocks.note: Apple's machines are Macs, short for Macintosh, and climbing the column the plural arrives this way round

annotation.surface: Apple machines being carried off in the course of a swindle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' reads as shoplifting in the surface and is the turn instruction in the parse. Down the grid that is the only wording available: there is no backwards on a vertical axis, only up.
annotation.definitionFit: A scam is a dishonest scheme for parting somebody from their money, which is exactly what a con is.

entries.clue: Last bit of wine – private room – paradise! (4)

indicatorNotes.Last bit of: The last bit of a word is the single letter it finishes on, not a syllable or a half.

blocks.note: the letter the word wine ends on
a den is the small room someone keeps to themselves at home

annotation.surface: The last of the bottle drunk in a study, and it feels like heaven.
annotation.walkthrough: The dashes make the clue look like three separate thoughts, and two of them are wordplay. Eden is the garden of Genesis, which is where English gets the word for any perfect place.
annotation.definitionFit: Eden is the garden of Genesis, and its name has long stood for any place of perfect ease — a paradise.

entries.clue: Frank in tennis championship? (4)

blocks.note: speaking without concealment, saying straight out what you think
the kind of tournament amateurs and professionals may both enter, and the word is its name

annotation.surface: Somebody being refreshingly candid in the middle of a tennis tournament.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Frank' wears a capital because it opens the sentence, not because it is a man's name, and that is the trap. One half of the pair is an adjective and the other a noun, which is all the answer needs to be both.
annotation.definitionFit: Open means frank when said of a person, and an Open is the tennis title anyone may enter, amateur or professional — Wimbledon has been one since 1968.

entries.clue: In stomped University College head, now and again brought into use (10)

indicatorNotes.now and again: What happens now and again happens at intervals with gaps between, so letters are taken from the word at every other step.

blocks.note: the word is taken exactly as printed
to have stomped on something is to have trod on it
the single letter a university is shortened to
the single letter a college is shortened to
the second and fourth letters of the four-letter word, the first and third skipped over

annotation.surface: The head of University College stamping into a room in a temper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'University College head' reads as one person and breaks into three separate pieces. 'Now and again' looks like a remark on how often he does it and is the instruction for picking letters out.
annotation.definitionFit: To introduce a law or a machine is to bring it in for the first time, which is the same act in the same tense.

entries.clue: Everyman’s eating spot of acrid duck sauce (4)

indicatorNotes.eating: Whatever is eating something has it inside, swallowed whole.
indicatorNotes.spot of: A spot of a thing is the smallest amount of it, and the smallest amount of a word is the letter it starts on.

blocks.note: the setter signs himself Everyman, so what belongs to Everyman is his own, written in the first person
the opening letter of the word acrid
a duck is a batsman's score of nought in cricket, and nought is written as a round letter

annotation.surface: The café where Everyman eats, and the sharp-tasting duck it serves.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eating spot' reads as a café and is two separate instructions sitting side by side. Everyman writes himself into his own puzzles most weeks, which is a convention worth learning early.
annotation.definitionFit: Mayo is the everyday short form of mayonnaise, the thick egg-and-oil dressing, so 'sauce' names it by kind.

entries.clue: Artist to draw outline of the old mine? Almost (6,4)

indicatorNotes.Almost: Almost the whole word means everything of it bar the letter at the end.

blocks.note: to draw the outline of something through thin paper laid over it is to trace it
ye is the antique spelling of 'the', as on a ye olde tea shoppe sign
the word for a pit dug for coal, with the last letter taken off it

annotation.surface: Someone sketching the shape of a disused pit, or very nearly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The old' is the antique definite article rather than a comment on the pit's age, and it is the join nobody sees. Tracey Emin is the British artist of My Bed and the neon texts, and a Royal Academician.
annotation.definitionFit: Tracey Emin is a British artist known for confessional work — the unmade bed, the appliquéd tent, the neon slogans — so 'Artist' names her by trade.
